section.heading: 7.2 Quadratic Forms
section.paragraph: Until now, our attention in this text has focused on linear equations, except for the sums of squares encountered in Chapter 6 when computing $$\textbf{x}^{T}\textbf{x}$$ . Such sums and more general expressions, called quadratic forms, occur frequently in applications of linear algebra to engineering (in design criteria and optimization) and signal processing (as output noise power). They also arise, for example, in physics (as potential and kinetic energy), differential geometry (as normal curvature of surfaces), economics (as utility functions), and statistics (in confidence ellipsoids). Some of the mathematical background for such applications flows easily from our work on symmetric matrices.

A quadratic form on $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ is a function $$Q$$ defined on $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ whose value at a vector $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ can be computed by an expression of the form $$Q(\textbf{x}) = \textbf{x}^{T} A\textbf{x}$$ , where $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ symmetric matrix. The matrix $$A$$ is called the matrix of the quadratic form.

The simplest example of a nonzero quadratic form is $$Q(\textbf{x}) = \textbf{x}^{T}I\textbf{x} = \text{∥} \textbf{x} \text{∥} ^{2}$$ . Examples 1 and 2 show the connection between any symmetric matrix $$A$$ and the quadratic form $$\textbf{x}^{T} A\textbf{x}$$ .

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$ . Compute $$\textbf{x}^{T} A\textbf{x}$$ for the following matrices:
example.heading: Solution

list.item: $$\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x} = \lbrack\begin{matrix} x_{1} & x_{2} \end{matrix}\rbrack\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \lbrack\begin{matrix} x_{1} & x_{2} \end{matrix}\rbrack\begin{bmatrix} {4x_{1}} \\ {3x_{2}} \end{bmatrix} = 4x_{1}^{2} + 3x_{2}^{2}$$ .

There are two $$- 2$$ entries in $$A$$ . Watch how they enter the calculations. The $$(1,2) \text{-entry}$$ in $$A$$ is in boldface type. $$\textbf{x}^{T} A \textbf{x} & = & [ x_{1} x_{2} ] \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 & - 2 \\ - 2 & 7\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = [ x_{1} x_{2} ] \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 x_{1} - 2 x_{2} \\ - 2 x_{1} + 7 x_{2}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & x_{1} \left(\right. 3 x_{1} - 2 x_{2} \left.\right) + x_{2} \left(\right. - 2 x_{1} + 7 x_{2} \left.\right) & = & 3 x_{1}^{2} - 2 x_{1} x_{2} - 2 x_{2} x_{1} + 7 x_{2}^{2} & = & 3 x_{1}^{2} - 4 x_{1} x_{2} + 7 x_{2}^{2}$$

section.paragraph: The presence of $$- 4x_{1}x_{2}$$ in the quadratic form in Example 1(b) is due to the $$- 2$$ entries off the diagonal in the matrix $$A$$ . In contrast, the quadratic form associated with the diagonal matrix $$A$$ in Example 1(a) has no $$x_{1} x_{2}$$ cross-product term.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: For $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , let $$Q(\textbf{x}) = 5x_{1}^{2} + 3x_{2}^{2} + 2x_{3}^{2} - x_{1}x_{2} + 8x_{2}x_{3}$$ . Write this quadratic form as $$\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The coefficients of $$x_{1}^{2}$$ , $$x_{2}^{2}$$ , $$x_{3}^{2}$$ go on the diagonal of $$A$$ . To make $$A$$ symmetric, the coefficient of $$x_{i}x_{j}$$ for $$i \neq j$$ must be split evenly between the $$(i,j)-$$ and $$(j,i) \text{-entries}$$ in $$A$$ . The coefficient of $$x_{1}x_{3}$$ is $$0$$ . It is readily checked that
$$Q ( \textbf{x} ) = \textbf{x}^{T} A \textbf{x} = [ x_{1} x_{2} x_{3} ] \left[\right. 5 & - 1 / 2 & 0 - 1 / 2 & 3 & 4 0 & 4 & 2 \left]\right. \left[\right. x_{1} x_{2} x_{3} \left]\right.$$

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Let $$Q(\textbf{x}) = x_{1}^{2} - 8x_{1}x_{2} - 5x_{2}^{2}$$ . Compute the value of $$Q(\textbf{x})$$ for $$\textbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: $$Q \left(\right. - 3 , 1 \left.\right) & = \left(\right. - 3 \left.\right)^{2} - 8 \left(\right. - 3 \left.\right) \left(\right. 1 \left.\right) - 5 \left(\right. 1 \left.\right)^{2} = 28 Q \left(\right. 2 , - 2 \left.\right) & = \left(\right. 2 \left.\right)^{2} - 8 \left(\right. 2 \left.\right) \left(\right. - 2 \left.\right) - 5 \left(\right. - 2 \left.\right)^{2} = 16 Q \left(\right. 1 , - 3 \left.\right) & = \left(\right. 1 \left.\right)^{2} - 8 \left(\right. 1 \left.\right) \left(\right. - 3 \left.\right) - 5 \left(\right. - 3 \left.\right)^{2} = - 20$$

section.paragraph: In some cases, quadratic forms are easier to use when they have no cross-product terms—that is, when the matrix of the quadratic form is a diagonal matrix. Fortunately, the cross-product term can be eliminated by making a suitable change of variable.
section.heading: Change of Variable in a Quadratic Form
section.paragraph: If $$\textbf{x}$$ represents a variable vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then a change of variable is an equation of the form
$$\textbf{x} = P \textbf{y} , \text{or equivalently} , \textbf{y} = P^{- 1} \textbf{x}$$

where $$P$$ is an invertible matrix and $$\textbf{y}$$ is a new variable vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Here $$\textbf{y}$$ is the coordinate vector of $$\textbf{x}$$ relative to the basis of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ determined by the columns of $$P$$ . (See Section 4.4.)
If the change of variable (1) is made in a quadratic form $$\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$$ , then

$$\textbf{x}^{T} A \textbf{x} = \left(\right. P \textbf{y} \left.\right) ^{T} A \left(\right. P \textbf{y} \left.\right) = \textbf{y}^{T} P^{T} A P \textbf{y} = \textbf{y}^{T} \left(\right. P^{T} A P \left.\right) \textbf{y}$$

and the new matrix of the quadratic form is $$P^{T}AP$$ . Since $$A$$ is symmetric, Theorem 2 guarantees that there is an orthogonal matrix $$P$$ such that $$P^{T}AP$$ is a diagonal matrix $$D$$ , and the quadratic form in (2) becomes $$\textbf{y}^{T}D\textbf{y}$$ . This is the strategy of the next example.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Make a change of variable that transforms the quadratic form in Example 3 into a quadratic form with no cross-product term.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The matrix of the quadratic form in Example 3 is
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 4 \\ - 4 & - 5 \end{bmatrix}$$
The first step is to orthogonally diagonalize $$A$$ . Its eigenvalues turn out to be $$\text{λ} = 3$$ and $$\text{λ} = - 7$$ . Associated unit eigenvectors are
$$\lambda = 3 : \begin{bmatrix} 2 / \sqrt{5} \\ - 1 / \sqrt{5} \end{bmatrix} ; \lambda = - 7 : \begin{bmatrix} 1 / \sqrt{5} \\ 2 / \sqrt{5} \end{bmatrix}$$
These vectors are automatically orthogonal (because they correspond to distinct eigenvalues) and so provide an orthonormal basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ . Let
$$P = \begin{bmatrix} 2 / \sqrt{5} & 1 / \sqrt{5} \\ - 1 / \sqrt{5} & 2 / \sqrt{5} \end{bmatrix} , D = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & - 7 \end{bmatrix}$$
Then $$A = {PDP}^{- 1}$$ and $$D = P^{- 1}{AP} = P^{T}AP$$ , as pointed out earlier. A suitable change of variable is
$$\textbf{x} = P \textbf{y} , \text{where} \textbf{x} = \left[\right. x_{1} x_{2} \left]\right. \text{and} \textbf{y} = \left[\right. y_{1} y_{2} \left]\right.$$
Then

$$x_{1}^{2} - 8 x_{1} x_{2} - 5 x_{2}^{2} & = \textbf{x}^{T} A \textbf{x} = \left(\right. P \textbf{y} \left.\right) ^{T} A \left(\right. P \textbf{y} \left.\right) & = \textbf{y}^{T} P^{T} A P \textbf{y} = \textbf{y}^{T} D \textbf{y} & = 3 y_{1}^{2} - 7 y_{2}^{2}$$

section.paragraph: To illustrate the meaning of the equality of quadratic forms in Example 4, we can compute $$Q(\textbf{x})$$ for $$\textbf{x} = (2, - 2)$$ using the new quadratic form. First, since $$\textbf{x} = P\textbf{y}$$ ,
$$\textbf{y} = P^{- 1} \textbf{x} = P^{T} \textbf{x}$$
so

$$\textbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 / \sqrt{5} & - 1 / \sqrt{5} \\ 1 / \sqrt{5} & 2 / \sqrt{5} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ - 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 / \sqrt{5} \\ - 2 / \sqrt{5} \end{bmatrix}$$
Hence

$$3 y_{1}^{2} - 7 y_{2}^{2} & = 3 \left(\right. 6 / \sqrt{5} \left.\right)^{2} - 7 \left(\right. - 2 / \sqrt{5} \left.\right)^{2} = 3 \left(\right. 36 / 5 \left.\right) - 7 \left(\right. 4 / 5 \left.\right) & = 80 / 5 = 16$$
This is the value of $$Q(\textbf{x})$$ in Example 3 when $$\textbf{x} = (2, - 2)$$ . See Figure 1.

section.paragraph: Example 4 illustrates the following theorem. The proof of the theorem was essentially given before Example 4.

note.title: Theorem 4
note.heading: Theorem 4
The Principal Axes Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be an $$n \times n$$ symmetric matrix. Then there is an orthogonal change of variable, $$\textbf{x} = P\textbf{y}$$ , that transforms the quadratic form $$\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$$ into a quadratic form $$\textbf{y}^{T}D\textbf{y}$$ with no cross-product term.

section.paragraph: The columns of $$P$$ in the theorem are called the principal axes of the quadratic form $$\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$$ . The vector $$\textbf{y}$$ is the coordinate vector of $$\textbf{x}$$ relative to the orthonormal basis of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ given by these principal axes.
section.heading: A Geometric View of Principal Axes
section.paragraph: Suppose $$Q(\textbf{x}) = \textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$$ , where $$A$$ is an invertible $$2 \times 2$$ symmetric matrix, and let $$c$$ be a constant. It can be shown that the set of all $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ that satisfy
$$\textbf{x}^{T} A \textbf{x} = c$$

either corresponds to an ellipse (or circle), a hyperbola, two intersecting lines, or a single point, or contains no points at all. If $$A$$ is a diagonal matrix, the graph is in standard position, such as in Figure 2. If $$A$$ is not a diagonal matrix, the graph of equation (3) is

The positive $$y_{1} \text{-axis}$$ in Figure 3(b) is in the direction of the first column of the matrix $$P$$ in Example 4, and the positive $$y_{2} \text{-axis}$$ is in the direction of the second column of $$P$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: The ellipse in Figure 3(a) is the graph of the equation $$5x_{1}^{2} - 4x_{1}x_{2} + 5x_{2}^{2} = 48$$ . Find a change of variable that removes the cross-product term from the equation.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The matrix of the quadratic form is $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 5 & {- 2} \\ {- 2} & 5 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . The eigenvalues of $$A$$ turn out to be $$3$$ and $$7$$ , with corresponding unit eigenvectors
$$\textbf{u}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / \sqrt{2} \\ 1 / \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{u}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} - 1 / \sqrt{2} \\ 1 / \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}$$

Let $$P = [\begin{matrix} \textbf{u}_{1} & \textbf{u}_{2} \end{matrix}] = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} {1/\sqrt{2}} & {- 1/\sqrt{2}} \\ {1/\sqrt{2}} & {1/\sqrt{2}} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Then $$P$$ orthogonally diagonalizes $$A$$ , so the change of variable $$\textbf{x} = P\textbf{y}$$ produces the quadratic form $$\textbf{y}^{T}D\textbf{y} = 3y_{1}^{2} + 7y_{2}^{2}$$ . The new axes for this change of variable are shown in Figure 3(a).

section.heading: Classifying Quadratic Forms
section.paragraph: When $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix, the quadratic form $$Q(\textbf{x}) = \textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$$ is a real-valued function with domain $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Figure 4 displays the graphs of four quadratic forms with domain $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ . For each point $$\textbf{x} = (x_{1},x_{2})$$ in the domain of a quadratic form $$Q$$ , the graph displays the point $$(x_{1},x_{2},z)$$ where $$z = Q(\textbf{x})$$ . Notice that except at $$\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ , the values of $$Q(\textbf{x})$$ are all positive in Figure 4(a) and all negative in Figure 4(d). The horizontal cross-sections of the graphs are ellipses in Figures 4(a) and 4(d) and hyperbolas in Figure 4(c).

section.paragraph: The simple $$2 \times 2$$ examples in Figure 4 illustrate the following definitions.

section.paragraph: Also, $$Q$$ is said to be positive semidefinite if $$Q(\textbf{x}) \geq 0$$ for all $$\textbf{x}$$ , and to be negative semidefinite if $$Q(\textbf{x}) \leq 0$$ for all $$\textbf{x}$$ . The quadratic forms in parts (a) and (b) of Figure 4 are both positive semidefinite, but the form in (a) is better described as positive definite.
Theorem 5 characterizes some quadratic forms in terms of eigenvalues.

note.title: Theorem 5
note.heading: Theorem 5
Quadratic Forms and Eigenvalues
note.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be an $$n \times n$$ symmetric matrix. Then a quadratic form $$\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$$ is

list.item: positive definite if and only if the eigenvalues of $$A$$ are all positive,
negative definite if and only if the eigenvalues of $$A$$ are all negative, or
indefinite if and only if $$A$$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

section.heading: Proof﻿
section.paragraph: By the Principal Axes Theorem, there exists an orthogonal change of variable $$\textbf{x} = P\textbf{y}$$ such that
$$Q \left(\right. \textbf{x} \left.\right) = \textbf{x}^{T} A \textbf{x} = \textbf{y}^{T} D \textbf{y} = \lambda_{1} y_{1}^{2} + \lambda_{2} y_{2}^{2} + \hdots + \lambda_{n} y_{n}^{2}$$

Since $$P$$ is invertible, there is a one-to-one correspondence between all nonzero $$\textbf{x}$$ and all nonzero $$\textbf{y}$$ . Thus the values of $$Q(\textbf{x})$$ for $$\textbf{x} \neq \textbf{0}$$ coincide with the values of the expression on the right side of (4), which is obviously controlled by the signs of the eigenvalues $$\text{λ} _{1},\ldots, \text{λ} _{n}$$ , in the three ways described in the theorem.

example.heading: Example 6
Solution
example.paragraph: Because of all the plus signs, this form “looks” positive definite. But the matrix of the form is
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
and the eigenvalues of $$A$$ turn out to be $$5$$ , $$2$$ , and $$- 1$$ . So $$Q$$ is an indefinite quadratic form, not positive definite.

section.paragraph: The classification of a quadratic form is often carried over to the matrix of the form. Thus a positive definite matrix ﻿ $$A$$ is a symmetric matrix for which the quadratic form $$\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$$ is positive definite. Other terms, such as positive semidefinite matrix, are defined analogously.

note.title: Numerical Notes
note.heading: Numerical Notes
note.paragraph: A fast way to determine whether a symmetric matrix $$A$$ is positive definite is to attempt to factor $$A$$ in the form $$A = R^{T}R$$ , where $$R$$ is upper triangular with positive diagonal entries. (A slightly modified algorithm for an LU factorization is one approach.) Such a Cholesky factorization is possible if and only if $$A$$ is positive definite. See Supplementary Exercise 23 at the end of Chapter 7.
